extracted.intended_audience: scholars and researchers in humor studies, linguistics, and prosody (people studying joke performance)
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical measurement and evaluation of timing in spoken joke performance, operationalized as pauses and rate of speech, comparing punch line vs. setup within speakers and across prepared/spontaneous conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing defined as pauses and rate of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: When we speak of “timing” in the performance of humorous narratives we mean only the distribution of pauses before the punch line and the rate of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This study excludes interactional definitions and paralinguistic markers (e.g., smiling voice, laughter). Other prosodic aspects (pitch, volume) may be relevant but are not the primary operationalization here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pause taxonomy / thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Brown et al. (1980) taxonomy of pauses: Very short pauses 0.2–0.4 seconds; Short pauses 0.4–0.6 seconds; Substantial pauses 0.6–0.8 seconds; Topic pauses greater than 0.8 seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature often claims pauses up to 30 seconds; however, for empirical testing the authors 'decided more reasonably to assume that punch lines would be signaled by substantial pauses or longer.' Use these thresholds to classify pauses and to operationalize 'noticeable' or 'substantial' pauses before punch lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech rate (syllables per second)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faster delivery can be operationalized as faster rate of speech measured in syllables per second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate speech rate for baseline and punch-line segments. Compare punch-line rate to baseline; typical adult English rates range ~3.47–5.7 syl/sec depending on condition. Use entire-text or sampled comparable segments; report means and test for statistical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation rate (speech rate minus pauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to speech rate as ascertained by syllables per second, calculate articulation rate: total time of a section minus pause time divided by the number of syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulation rate controls for pause time; useful when pauses differ between setup and punch line. As with speech rate, compare within-speaker baseline vs punch line to control inter-individual voice differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch line identification (Hockett/Attardo method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch lines were identified using the standard Hockett (1973; 1977) method, as amended by Attardo (1994), and using semantic analysis: the analyst starts removing phrases from the end of the text and checks whether the humorous effect is still present; when the humorous effect is no longer present this indicates the last phrase removed was the punch line; semantic analysis then confirms the test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this iterative removal + semantic confirmation approach to locate the punch line reliably, especially when punch lines are short and pose measurement challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline selection for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: A baseline speech rate was established by calculating the rate of an earlier section of the narrative comparable to the punch line in terms of length and prominent syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an earlier segment matched in length/prominence to the punch-line segment to form a fair baseline; if the punch line is too short for reliable measurement, include a preceding portion for rate calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-speaker comparisons to control inter-individual variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Since significant variation exists among individuals, prosodic differences were measured between the punch line and the setup of the same joke to ensure that no inter-individual variation affected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always compare baseline vs punch line measurements for the same speaker (rather than across speakers) to control for voice/pitch/tempo differences (e.g., gender differences in pitch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental acoustic analysis and data quality inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Data were subject to instrumental analysis using the pitch extraction function of a Kaypentax Computerized Speech Laboratory (CSL). Instrumental analysis constrained usable recordings; many recordings contained too much ambient noise to constitute reliable data for instrumental analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include recordings with sufficient signal-to-noise for reliable acoustic measurement; document equipment and functions used (e.g., CSL pitch extraction). Discard contaminated cases (e.g., operator laughter) and report selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: pause before punch line
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis: There is a pause before the punch line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize this as a systematic occurrence of noticeable/substantial pauses immediately before punch lines; test by measuring pause duration preceding punch lines vs. setup. Paper finds hypothesis falsified in their data (no systematic emphatic pause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: punch lines delivered with altered rate/clip
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis: Punch lines are delivered faster (Norrick 2001), more clipped (Bauman 1986), and 'with bells and whistles' (Chafe 1994) than non-punch lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by comparing speech/articulation rate of punch lines vs. baseline; consider clipped delivery and rapidity as acoustic correlates. In this study, punch lines were not significantly faster; articulation rate differences were not statistically significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: shift in voice quality (pitch/volume) at punch line
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a shift in voice quality (pitch) and volume at the punch line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although recognized as relevant, pitch and volume shifts were noted but 'these aspects are not pursued in this paper.' If pursued, measure pitch and intensity changes and consider reported-speech marking (higher pitch/louder) and prominence/focality manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported speech as a variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported speech has previously been connected to the production of a faster rate in punch lines; compare punch lines that occur in reported speech with those that do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize samples by whether the punch line occurs in reported speech and test for differences in rate/pause. Note sample-size limitations: here only two non-reported-speech examples existed and no significant difference was found (Mann-Whitney p=0.5333); treat conclusions as tentative when applicable sample is small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepared vs. spontaneous jokes comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare prepared (rehearsed) versus spontaneous (improvised) jokes for differences in timing parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study there were no significant differences between prepared and improvised jokes across timing measures; the result suggests researchers may assign jokes to speakers when investigating timing variables, but further work (including professionals) is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for performance errors and their impact
rubrics_metrics.description: High frequency of serious performance errors (hesitations, disfluencies, substitutions) can occur at or near punch lines and can destroy the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and analyze performance errors (e.g., filled pauses, long hesitations, slips) and consider their relation to joke comprehension and prosodic measures; be aware that speakers correct toward an idealized competence joke, and errors may bias timing measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical testing and sample-size caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate statistical tests to compare timing measures and be cautious about generalization given sample composition (e.g., undergraduate students, number of tokens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report means, test for statistical significance (e.g., Mann-Whitney for small samples), and acknowledge limitations (small N, selection by recording quality). Avoid overgeneralizing; plan follow-up studies with professionals or different elicitation contexts to validate findings.
